options: There are several possible causes, and they may differ from place to place
The first farmers wrote down their reasons in different languages
All the evidence has been lost

parts_head.eyebrow: Try It in the Model · 在模型裡試試

parts.text_en: Watch the foragers' camp. It moves to the river, the meadow, the woods, and a sheltered winter spot. People go to the food. Everything they own has to be carried.
parts.text_zh: 看採集狩獵者的營地。它搬到河邊、草地、樹林，再搬到背風的地方過冬。人去找食物。他們擁有的每一樣東西都得搬得動。

parts.en: The field that cannot be left
parts.text_en: Watch one field from sowing to harvest. The farmers bring the food to themselves, but the field needs them for months, and the village stays where the field is.
parts.text_zh: 看一塊田從播種到收割。農人讓食物長在自己身邊，但是田有好幾個月都需要人照顧，而田在哪裡，村子就留在哪裡。

parts.text_en: After the harvest the granary is full, and it empties a little every day until the next one. Stored food carries a village through winter. It can also be counted, guarded, and owned.
parts.text_zh: 收割之後穀倉是滿的，然後每天少一點，一直到下一次收成。存糧讓村子撐過冬天。存糧也可以被清點、被看守、被擁有。

parts.meta_en: Switch on “A year when the harvest fails”
parts.text_en: Switch on the bad year and go to spring. The granary is empty before the new crop is ready. Compare how each bank gets through.
parts.text_zh: 打開歉收的一年，再跳到春天。新的作物還沒熟，穀倉已經空了。比較一下兩岸各自怎麼撐過去。

lessons.parts_note_en: The model shows a pattern, not a rule. After you have watched it, read the note under the picture about what it leaves out.
lessons.parts_note_zh: 模型呈現的是一種常見的情形，不是定律。看完以後，讀一讀圖下面那段說明，看它省略了什麼。

centers.lead_en: Pull the slider from 12,000 years ago toward the present. A region glows faintly when the earliest evidence appears there, and strongly once farming is clearly under way. People in these regions did not learn farming from one another: each worked it out with the plants that grew nearby. Click a number to see what was grown there.
centers.lead_zh: 把滑桿從 1.2 萬年前往現在拉。一個地區出現最早的證據時會淡淡地亮起來，等到那裡的農業已經很明確了，才變成實的。這些地區的人不是互相學來的：每個地方的人都是用身邊長的植物，自己摸索出來的。點一個號碼，看那裡種的是什麼。
centers.idle_en: Click a numbered circle on the map, or a name below it.
centers.idle_zh: 點地圖上有號碼的圓，或是地圖下面的名字。
centers.foot_en: The map shows seven regions whose dates this lesson could check against published studies. A 2014 review counts at least eleven regions where farming began independently, and several more have been proposed. The glow marks a rough area, not a border, and each date is a range that new finds may change.
centers.foot_zh: 地圖上畫的是七個地區，它們的年代這一課都對過已發表的研究。2014 年的一篇綜述認為農業至少在十一個地區各自獨立開始，另外還有幾個地區有人主張。光暈只表示「大約這一帶」，不是邊界；每一個年代都是一段範圍，新的發現可能會改動它。

centers.crops_en: Wheat and barley, and herd animals at about the same time.
centers.crops_zh: 小麥和大麥；大約同一個時期也開始飼養成群的牲畜。
centers.when_en: People were tending wild plants and animals by at least 11,500 years ago. Wheat that keeps its seeds on the stalk, a sign of domestication, appears about 9,500 years ago.
centers.when_zh: 至少在 1.15 萬年前，人們已經在照管野生的植物和動物。種子不會自己掉落的小麥（馴化的記號）大約 9,500 年前出現。
centers.note_en: This region is often called the Fertile Crescent. Even here there was no single starting point: crops were domesticated slowly, in several places.
centers.note_zh: 這個地區常被稱為肥沃月彎。就算在這裡，也沒有單一的起點：作物是在好幾個地方慢慢馴化的。
centers.src: Zeder, Current Anthropology (2011); Tanno and Willcox, Science (2006)

centers.when_en: Broomcorn millet from about 10,300 to 8,700 years ago at one site, although some archaeologists have questioned those dates. A 2024 study places the domestication of millets anywhere between about 10,300 and 6,300 years ago.
centers.when_zh: 有一處遺址的黍大約是 1.03 萬到 8,700 年前的，不過有考古學家對這個年代有疑問。2024 年的一項研究把黍和小米馴化的時間放在大約 1.03 萬到 6,300 年前之間。
centers.src: Lu et al., PNAS (2009); Stevens, Zhuang, and Fuller, Evolutionary Human Sciences (2024)

centers.when_en: Rice remains about 9,400 years old suggest that domestication may have begun by then. At a later site, 6,900 to 6,600 years ago, fewer than half of the rice remains yet showed the domesticated form.
centers.when_zh: 大約 9,400 年前的稻遺留顯示，馴化可能那時候就開始了。在比較晚的一處遺址（6,900 到 6,600 年前），帶有馴化特徵的稻還不到一半。
centers.note_en: The two results are not in conflict. Together they show how long the change took.
centers.note_zh: 這兩個結果並不衝突，合起來正好說明這個變化花了多久。
centers.src: Zuo et al., PNAS (2017); Fuller et al., Science (2009)

centers.when_en: Squash was grown between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago. Maize was present by 8,700 years ago.
centers.when_zh: 南瓜在 1 萬到 8,000 年前之間已經有人栽培。8,700 年前已經有玉米。
centers.src: Smith, Science (1997); Piperno et al., PNAS (2009)

centers.crops_en: Squash first; peanuts and cotton later.
centers.crops_zh: 先是南瓜，後來有花生和棉花。
centers.when_en: In one valley on the western slopes of the Andes in northern Peru, people were growing squash by about 10,000 years ago. Peanuts and cotton appear later in the same valley.
centers.when_zh: 在秘魯北部安地斯山西坡的一座河谷，大約 1 萬年前已經有人種南瓜。花生和棉花比較晚才出現在同一座河谷。
centers.note_en: The circle marks where these remains were found. Other South American crops were domesticated in other parts of the continent.
centers.note_zh: 圓圈標的是這些遺留出土的地方。南美洲其他的作物，是在這塊大陸的其他地方馴化的。

centers.when_en: People were using and perhaps planting these plants about 10,000 years ago. Mounded garden beds, clear evidence of farming, date from about 6,950 to 6,440 years ago.
centers.when_zh: 大約 1 萬年前，人們已經在利用（也許已經在種）這些植物。堆成土丘的菜圃是農業的明確證據，年代大約是 6,950 到 6,440 年前。
centers.note_en: The site, Kuk Swamp, is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
centers.note_zh: 這處遺址（庫克沼澤）列在聯合國教科文組織的世界遺產名錄上。
centers.src: Denham et al., Science (2003); UNESCO World Heritage Centre

centers.crops_en: Sorghum in the east; pearl millet in the west.
centers.crops_zh: 東邊是高粱，西邊是珍珠粟。
centers.when_en: In the eastern Sahel, sorghum shows domesticated traits about 6,000 to 5,000 years ago. For pearl millet, genetic studies point to the western Sahel by about 4,800 years ago, and the oldest plant remains with domesticated traits are about 4,500 years old.
centers.when_zh: 在薩赫爾地區東部，高粱大約在 6,000 到 5,000 年前出現馴化的特徵。至於珍珠粟，基因研究指向大約 4,800 年前的薩赫爾西部，而帶有馴化特徵的最古老植物遺留大約是 4,500 年前的。
centers.note_en: The Sahel is the belt of dry grassland along the southern edge of the Sahara.
centers.note_zh: 薩赫爾是撒哈拉沙漠南緣的一條乾燥草原帶。
centers.src: Winchell et al., Current Anthropology (2017); Jiménez-Arteaga et al., Scientific Reports (2025)

match.lead_en: Eight foods you may have eaten this week. Where were they first farmed? Use the map above if you need it. There is no timer, and you can keep choosing until you get it; the game counts how many you place correctly on the first try.
match.lead_zh: 八種你這個星期可能吃過的食物。它們最早是在哪裡被人栽培的？需要的話可以看上面的地圖。不計時，可以一直選到對為止；遊戲會記下你第一次就選對的題數。
match.ask_zh: 這種作物最早在哪裡被人栽培？

items.en: Rice, in your lunch box
items.why_en: Rice was domesticated along the lower Yangtze, over thousands of years.
items.why_zh: 稻是在長江下游，花了幾千年慢慢馴化的。
items.hint_en: Think of a warm, wet river valley in East Asia.
items.hint_zh: 想想東亞一條又暖又濕的大河流域。

items.en: Wheat, in bread and noodles
items.why_en: Wheat and barley were domesticated in West Asia.
items.why_zh: 小麥和大麥是在西亞馴化的。
items.hint_en: The region is often called the Fertile Crescent.
items.hint_zh: 這個地區常被叫做肥沃月彎。

items.en: Maize (corn)
items.why_en: Maize was being grown in what is now southwestern Mexico by 8,700 years ago.
items.why_zh: 8,700 年前，今天墨西哥西南部一帶已經有人種玉米。
items.hint_en: Not in Asia, Africa, or Europe.
items.hint_zh: 不在亞洲、非洲，也不在歐洲。

items.en: Millet, the small yellow grain
items.why_en: Broomcorn millet and foxtail millet were the first grain crops of dry northern China.
items.why_zh: 黍和小米（粟）是乾燥的華北最早的穀類作物。
items.hint_en: It grows where there is too little rain for rice.
items.hint_zh: 它長在雨水不夠種稻的地方。

items.en: Peanuts
items.why_en: The oldest peanut remains found so far come from northern Peru. Exactly where on the continent peanuts were first grown is less certain.
items.why_zh: 目前找到最古老的花生遺留出自秘魯北部。至於花生最早是在這塊大陸的哪裡被人栽培的，就比較不確定了。
items.hint_en: Not Asia, and not Africa.
items.hint_zh: 不是亞洲，也不是非洲。

items.en: Bananas
items.why_en: Bananas were being cultivated in the highlands of New Guinea about 7,000 years ago.
items.why_zh: 大約 7,000 年前，新幾內亞高地已經有人栽培香蕉。
items.hint_en: A large island north of Australia.
items.hint_zh: 澳洲北邊的一座大島。

items.en: Sorghum
items.why_en: Sorghum was domesticated in the eastern Sahel, the dry grassland south of the Sahara.
items.why_zh: 高粱是在薩赫爾地區東部（撒哈拉沙漠以南的乾燥草原）馴化的。
items.hint_en: A grain that stands up to heat and drought.
items.hint_zh: 一種耐熱又耐旱的穀物。

items.en: Squash and pumpkins
items.why_en: Different kinds of squash were domesticated separately: one in Mesoamerica, another in South America, and another in eastern North America. The same idea, more than once.
items.why_zh: 不同種類的南瓜是分別馴化的：一種在中部美洲，一種在南美洲，還有一種在北美洲東部。同一個點子，不只出現一次。
items.hint_en: Look at the map: it appears in more than one card.
items.hint_zh: 看看地圖：它出現在不只一張卡上。

match.end_en: No single region gave the world its food. A bowl of rice, a slice of bread, and a handful of peanuts are three separate inventions from three parts of the world.
match.end_zh: 世界上的食物不是哪一個地區單獨給的。一碗飯、一片麵包、一把花生，是世界上三個地方各自的發明。

gains.lead_en: When people took up farming, some things went up, some went down, and some are still argued over. Sort each one by what the evidence shows. The point is not to decide whether farming was good or bad. It is to see that it was a trade.
gains.lead_zh: 人開始種田以後，有些事增加了，有些事減少了，有些到現在還在爭論。依照證據顯示的結果，把每一項分好。重點不是判定農業是好是壞，而是看到它是一場交換。
gains.ask_en: After farming began, what happened to this?
gains.ask_zh: 開始種田以後，這一項怎麼了？

items.en: The share of children among the people buried in cemeteries
items.zh: 墓地裡，孩子在所有被埋葬的人當中占的比例
items.why_en: Burial grounds from after farming began hold a clearly larger share of children's skeletons. One researcher reads this as about two more births per woman. What exactly the change means is still discussed.
items.why_zh: 農業開始以後的墓地裡，孩子的骨骸占的比例明顯變高。有一位研究者把它解讀成每位婦女大約多生兩個孩子。這個變化到底代表什麼，還在討論中。
items.hint_en: Think about what settled life and stored grain make possible.
items.hint_zh: 想想定居和存糧讓什麼變得可能。

items.en: How tall adults grew, in most places studied
items.zh: 成年人的身高（在多數研究過的地方）
items.why_en: A review of many studies found that in most of them people became shorter as farming took hold, a sign of poorer nutrition or more illness in childhood.
items.why_zh: 一篇整理許多研究的回顧發現，大多數研究裡，人在農業站穩之後變矮了——這表示小時候營養比較差，或是比較常生病。
items.hint_en: Height is a record of how well a child ate.
items.hint_zh: 身高記錄了一個孩子小時候吃得好不好。

items.en: How far people moved during a year
items.zh: 人在一年裡移動的距離
items.why_en: Fields, stored grain, and houses hold people in one place. A study of bones from one early village in what is now Turkey found that people moved about less as they came to rely more on crops and herds.
items.why_zh: 田、存糧和房子把人留在一個地方。一項研究分析今天土耳其境內一處早期村落出土的骨骸，發現人越依賴作物和牲畜，移動得就越少。
items.hint_en: Watch the two banks of the river in the model.
items.hint_zh: 看看模型裡河的兩岸。

items.en: The gap between richer and poorer households
items.zh: 比較富有和比較貧窮的家庭之間的差距
items.why_en: A study of house sizes at many ancient sites found that differences in wealth generally grew after plants and animals were domesticated. Land, herds, and stored grain can be owned and handed down.
items.why_zh: 一項比較許多古代遺址房屋大小的研究發現，馴化動植物之後，貧富差距普遍變大。土地、牲畜和存糧可以被擁有，也可以傳給下一代。
items.hint_en: What can be owned when food is stored?
items.hint_zh: 食物可以存起來的時候，有什麼東西可以被「擁有」？

items.en: The hours of work in a day
items.why_en: A famous study of one group of foragers is often quoted for how few hours they spent getting food, but that figure leaves out preparing and cooking it. A study of one people in the Philippines found that those who farmed more had less free time. No single answer fits everyone.
items.why_zh: 有一項針對某一群採集狩獵者的著名研究，常被引用來說明他們花在找食物上的時間很少，但那個數字沒有算進處理和烹煮食物的時間。菲律賓某一個族群的研究則發現，種田比較多的人空閒時間比較少。沒有一個答案適用於所有人。
items.hint_en: It depends on what you count as work, and on whom you study.
items.hint_zh: 這要看什麼算是「工作」，也要看研究的是誰。

items.en: Whether life became better
items.why_en: One well-known scientist and author called farming “the worst mistake in the history of the human race.” Others point out that it fed far more people and that foragers had hard times too. The evidence can measure height and births. It cannot measure happiness.
items.why_zh: 有一位知名的科學家兼作家把農業稱為「人類歷史上最大的錯誤」。也有人指出，農業養活了多得多的人，而採集狩獵的人日子也有難過的時候。證據量得出身高和出生數，量不出幸福。
items.hint_en: Can a bone tell you whether someone was content?
items.hint_zh: 一根骨頭能告訴你一個人滿不滿足嗎？

gains.end_en: Farming was not simply progress, and it was not simply a mistake. It was a trade: more food and more people, in exchange for harder risks and less freedom to move. Different peoples made that trade at different times, and some did not make it at all.
gains.end_zh: 農業不單純是進步，也不單純是錯誤。它是一場交換：更多的食物、更多的人，換來的是更大的風險，和比較少的移動自由。不同的人群在不同的時候做了這個交換，也有人始終沒有換。

timeline.en: The same idea, in lane after lane
timeline.zh: 同一個點子，出現在一條又一條線上
timeline.lead_en: Each bar is the estimated range for the beginning of farming in one region. Read down the timeline: within a few thousand years, people far apart, who had not learned it from one another, were all doing something no human had done before. Two lanes are empty in this lesson. Farming reached Europe when farmers related to those of Anatolia, in West Asia, moved in; that is a story for a later lesson.
timeline.lead_zh: 每一條長條，是一個地區開始種田的估計範圍。直著讀這條時間軸：在幾千年之內，相隔遙遠、並沒有互相學習的人，都做起了一件以前沒有人做過的事。這一課有兩條線是空的。歐洲的農業，是和西亞安納托利亞的農人有親緣關係的農人搬進去的時候帶來的；那是後面的課要講的故事。
timeline.idle_en: Click a bar or a diamond to read its dates. Press “Whole span” to see how late in the human story all of this comes.
timeline.idle_zh: 點一條長條或一個菱形，讀出它的年代。按「全部」，看看這一切在人類的故事裡出現得有多晚。

tips.en: A long bar means a slow change, or an uncertain date, or both.
tips.zh: 長條很長，表示變化很慢，或是年代不確定，或是兩者都有。

tips.en: A striped bar marks a date that researchers still debate.
tips.zh: 有條紋的長條，是研究者還在爭論的年代。

tips.en: The gray diamond is something that came before farming: bread.
tips.zh: 灰色的菱形是比農業更早的事：麵包。

events.note_en: Foragers at a site in the Black Desert of Jordan baked flatbread from wild grain at least 4,000 years before farming began.
events.note_zh: 約旦黑沙漠一處遺址的採集狩獵者，用野生的穀子烤出了扁麵包，比農業開始早了至少 4,000 年。

events.note_en: People tended wild plants by at least 11,500 years ago. Domesticated wheat appears about 9,500 years ago.
events.note_zh: 至少 1.15 萬年前人們已經在照管野生植物；馴化的小麥大約 9,500 年前出現。

events.note_en: Broomcorn millet at one site. A 2024 study gives a wider range for millet domestication, 10,300 to 6,300 years ago.
events.note_zh: 一處遺址的黍。2024 年的研究給了更寬的範圍：1.03 萬到 6,300 年前。

events.note_en: Domestication may have begun about 9,400 years ago and was still under way 6,600 years ago.
events.note_zh: 馴化可能大約 9,400 年前開始，到 6,600 年前還在進行。

events.note_en: Charred grains from a site in what is now the Tainan Science Park.
events.note_zh: 出自今天臺南科學園區裡一處遺址的碳化穀粒。

events.en: Bananas and taro in New Guinea
events.zh: 新幾內亞的香蕉和芋頭
events.note_en: Use of these plants about 10,000 years ago; clear cultivation from about 6,950 to 6,440 years ago.
events.note_zh: 大約 1 萬年前已在利用這些植物；明確的栽培是大約 6,950 到 6,440 年前。

events.zh: 中部美洲的南瓜和玉米
events.note_en: Squash between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago; maize by 8,700 years ago.
events.note_zh: 南瓜在 1 萬到 8,000 年前之間；玉米最晚在 8,700 年前。

events.note_en: By about 10,000 years ago in northern Peru; peanuts and cotton came later.
events.note_zh: 大約 1 萬年前，在秘魯北部；花生和棉花比較晚。

events.note_en: Sorghum about 6,000 to 5,000 years ago; pearl millet by about 4,800 years ago.
events.note_zh: 高粱大約 6,000 到 5,000 年前；珍珠粟最晚大約 4,800 年前。

how_we_know.eyebrow: How Do We Know? · 我們怎麼知道？
how_we_know.en: Burned seeds, stubborn stalks, and specks of dust
how_we_know.zh: 燒焦的種子、不肯掉的穗，和一粒粒微塵
how_we_know.lead_en: No one wrote any of this down. The story of the first farmers is read from what they threw away, and most of it is very small.
how_we_know.lead_zh: 這些事沒有任何人寫下來。最早的農人的故事，是從他們丟掉的東西裡讀出來的，而且大部分都非常小。

items.en: Burned seeds
items.limit_en: Only what was burned survives, so foods that were never cooked near a fire, such as leaves and soft fruit, are nearly invisible.
items.limit_zh: 只有被燒過的才留得下來，所以從來不在火邊煮的食物（例如葉子和軟的果實）幾乎看不到。
items.text_en: Seeds that fell into a fire and turned to charcoal do not rot. Archaeologists stir soil from a site into water; the charred seeds float, and can be skimmed off and identified one by one. This is how the millet and rice of ancient Taiwan were found.
items.text_zh: 掉進火裡、燒成炭的種子不會腐爛。考古學家把遺址的土倒進水裡攪一攪，碳化的種子會浮起來，撈出來以後一粒一粒辨認。古代台灣的小米和稻就是這樣找到的。

items.en: Seeds that stay on the stalk
items.limit_en: This shows that a crop was changing, not when people first began to plant it. Planting came long before the plants looked different.
items.limit_zh: 這只能看出作物正在改變，看不出人是什麼時候開始種的。早在植物看起來不一樣之前很久，人就已經在種了。
items.text_en: On a wild plant, each grain in its husk falls off cleanly when ripe and leaves a smooth scar where it was attached. On a domesticated plant the grain has to be torn off by threshing, which leaves a rough scar. By counting smooth and rough scars under a microscope, researchers can tell how far a crop had changed.
items.text_zh: 野生的植株上，帶殼的穀粒熟了會整齊地脫落，在原本相連的地方留下光滑的疤。馴化的植株上，穀粒要靠打穀才扯得下來，留下的疤是粗糙的。在顯微鏡下數一數光滑的和粗糙的各有多少，研究者就知道一種作物已經改變了多少。

items.en: Traces too small to see
items.limit_en: Telling a wild plant from its domesticated relative by such traces takes great care, and specialists sometimes disagree about what a particle is.
items.limit_zh: 要靠這些痕跡分辨野生的植物和它馴化的親戚，需要非常小心；一顆顆粒到底是什麼，專家有時候看法也不同。
items.text_en: Plants leave behind microscopic grains of starch and tiny glassy particles called phytoliths, each kind with its own shape. They cling to grinding stones and cooking pots for thousands of years. Maize in Mexico was identified this way, on grinding stones and other stone tools from layers about 8,700 years old.
items.text_zh: 植物會留下顯微鏡才看得到的澱粉粒，以及叫做「植矽體」的玻璃質小顆粒，每一種植物的形狀都不一樣。它們可以黏在磨石和陶鍋上幾千年。墨西哥的玉米就是這樣認出來的——在大約 8,700 年前的地層出土的磨石和其他石器上。

views.en: Four questions without a settled answer
views.lead_en: The beginning of farming is one of the most argued-over questions in the study of the past. Here are four parts of the argument. The views are set side by side; this lesson does not choose between them.
views.lead_zh: 農業的開始，是研究過去的學問裡爭論最多的問題之一。下面是這場爭論的四個部分。各種說法並列，這一課不替誰下結論。
views.rule_en: Notice what kind of disagreement this is. Nobody disputes that farming began. The exact dates in each region are still argued over, and the hardest arguments are about why it began and what it did to people. On those questions the evidence speaks least clearly.
views.rule_zh: 留意這是哪一種分歧。沒有人否認農業開始了。每個地區確切的年代還在爭論，而最難的爭論是它為什麼開始、對人造成了什麼影響。在這些問題上，證據說得最不清楚。

items.topic_en: Why did people begin to farm?
items.topic_zh: 人為什麼開始種田？

sides.en: One influential paper argues that farming was impossible in the cold, unstable climate of the last ice age and became possible only when the climate steadied afterward.
sides.zh: 一篇很有影響力的論文主張：在上一次冰河時期又冷又不穩定的氣候下，農業根本不可能；要等之後氣候穩定下來，才變得可能。
sides.src: Richerson, Boyd, and Bettinger, American Antiquity 66 (2001)

sides.en: On the eastern shore of the Mediterranean, some foragers were living in long-lasting settlements 15,000 years ago, well before anyone farmed. House mice had already moved in with them. Researchers who stress this evidence argue that staying put came first and farming followed.
sides.zh: 在地中海東岸，有些採集狩獵者 1.5 萬年前就住在長期使用的聚落裡，比任何人開始種田都早得多。家鼠那時候已經搬進去和他們一起住了。重視這項證據的研究者主張：是先定居，然後才有農業。
sides.src: Weissbrod et al., PNAS 114 (2017)

sides.en: At Göbekli Tepe, in what is now southeastern Turkey, hunter-gatherers carved and raised decorated stone pillars. Its excavators described people coming together there for feasting, and suggested that such gatherings may have encouraged them to make more use of wild grain. Whether people also lived at the site is debated.
sides.zh: 在今天土耳其東南部的哥貝克力山丘，採集狩獵者雕刻並豎起了有裝飾的石柱。發掘它的考古學家描述人們聚在那裡舉行宴飲，並且提出：這樣的聚會可能促使人們更常利用野生的穀子。至於是不是也有人住在那裡，還有爭論。
sides.src: Dietrich et al., Antiquity 86 (2012)

items.note_en: Each idea has critics. A study of gazelle teeth from the eastern Mediterranean, for example, found that a cold spell there, long thought to have been dry as well, was not drier, which weakens one version of the climate story. Many researchers now doubt that one cause explains all eleven or more beginnings.
items.note_zh: 每一種想法都有人批評。例如，一項研究分析地中海東岸出土的瞪羚牙齒，發現那裡的一次變冷（長久以來被認為同時也變乾）其實並沒有比較乾，這削弱了氣候說的其中一個版本。現在很多研究者懷疑，有哪一個單一的原因能解釋十一個以上的開端。

items.topic_en: Was farming good for the people who did it?
items.topic_zh: 農業對種田的人是好事嗎？

sides.en: A review of many studies of skeletons found that in most of them people became shorter as farming took hold, and an earlier survey found health declining in 19 of 21 societies. In 1987 the scientist and author Jared Diamond called farming “the worst mistake in the history of the human race.”
sides.zh: 一篇整理許多骨骸研究的回顧發現，大多數研究裡，人在農業站穩之後變矮了；更早的一項調查則發現，21 個社會裡有 19 個的健康狀況變差。1987 年，科學家兼作家賈德・戴蒙把農業稱為「人類歷史上最大的錯誤」。
sides.src: Mummert et al., Economics and Human Biology 9 (2011)

sides.en: Burial grounds from the same period hold a larger share of children, which one researcher reads as about two more births per woman, and populations grew. Farming fed far more people from the same land. Other researchers also warn against imagining that foragers lived in ease.
sides.zh: 同一個時期的墓地裡，孩子占的比例變高——有一位研究者把它解讀成每位婦女大約多生兩個孩子——人口也增加了。同一塊地，農業養活的人多得多。也有研究者提醒，不要把採集狩獵者的生活想像得很輕鬆。
sides.src: Bocquet-Appel, Science 333 (2011); Kaplan, Journal of Anthropological Research 56 (2000)

items.note_en: Both sets of facts can be true together: more people, living in poorer health. Whether that is “better” depends on what is being weighed, and that is a question evidence alone cannot settle.
items.note_zh: 兩組事實可以同時成立：人變多了，健康卻變差了。這算不算「更好」，要看拿什麼來衡量——而這個問題，光靠證據回答不了。

items.topic_en: Did foragers work less than farmers?
items.topic_zh: 採集狩獵者的工作時間比農人少嗎？

sides.en: A study in the 1960s of one group of foragers in southern Africa is often quoted as showing that they spent only about 15 to 20 hours a week getting food. It gave rise to the idea that foragers lived with plenty of free time. A 2019 study of one people in the Philippines found that those who farmed more had less leisure.
sides.zh: 1960 年代對非洲南部一群採集狩獵者的研究，常被引用來說明他們每個星期只花大約 15 到 20 小時找食物，於是有了「採集狩獵者有很多空閒時間」的說法。2019 年對菲律賓某一個族群的研究則發現，種田比較多的人，空閒時間比較少。
sides.src: Dyble et al., Nature Human Behaviour 3 (2019)

sides.en: The often-quoted figure leaves out making tools and preparing and cooking the food. With those counted, the same study's total comes to more than 40 hours a week. Critics also ask how well fed those foragers really were.
sides.zh: 常被引用的那個數字沒有算進製作工具、處理和烹煮食物的時間。把這些算進去，同一項研究的總數超過每星期 40 小時。批評者也問：那些採集狩獵者實際上吃得夠不夠？
sides.src: Wikipedia, “Original affluent society” (an encyclopedia summary of the debate); Kaplan (2000)

items.note_en: Studies of living peoples cover only a few groups in particular places, and none of them lived 10,000 years ago. They are hints, not measurements of the past.
items.note_zh: 對現代族群的研究只涵蓋特定地方的少數幾群人，而且他們都不是活在一萬年前。這些是線索，不是對過去的測量。

items.topic_en: When did rice farming begin?
items.topic_zh: 稻作是什麼時候開始的？

sides.en: Microscopic plant particles from the Shangshan site near the lower Yangtze are about 9,400 years old, and their shape suggests that rice domestication may have begun by then.
sides.zh: 長江下游附近上山遺址的植物微粒大約是 9,400 年前的，從形狀看，稻的馴化可能那時候就開始了。
sides.src: Zuo et al., PNAS 114 (2017)

sides.en: At Tianluoshan, in the same region, the share of rice remains with the domesticated seed-holding trait rose only from 27 to 39 percent between 6,900 and 6,600 years ago. On this evidence rice was still mostly wild in form at that time.
sides.zh: 在同一個地區的田螺山遺址，6,900 到 6,600 年前之間，種子不會自己掉落（馴化特徵）的稻只從 27% 增加到 39%。照這份證據，那時候的稻在形態上大部分還是野生的。
sides.src: Fuller et al., Science 323 (2009)

items.note_en: The two studies measure different things, and they fit one picture: people may have been growing rice for a very long time before the plant itself finished changing. The earliest dates remain debated.
items.note_zh: 這兩項研究量的是不同的東西，卻拼得成同一幅圖：在稻這種植物本身變完之前，人可能已經種了很久很久。最早的年代仍然有爭論。

phrases.en: Eight sentences for causes, results, and slow change
phrases.zh: 說原因、說結果、說「慢慢地」的八句英文
phrases.lead_en: History is full of becauses, and careful writers do not claim more than they know. These sentences show how to give a possible reason, how to say what followed, and how to say that something happened slowly. Listen, repeat, then make your own sentence with the words in bold.
phrases.lead_zh: 歷史裡到處都是「因為」，而細心的寫作者不會說得比自己知道的更多。這八句示範怎麼提出一個可能的原因、怎麼說接下來發生了什麼、怎麼說一件事是慢慢發生的。先聽、再跟著唸，然後用粗體的字自己造一句。

rows.en: Before farming, people gathered wild plants and hunted.
rows.html: Before farming, people gathered wild plants and hunted.
rows.zh: 在有農業之前，人們採集野生的植物，也打獵。
rows.note_en: before + noun: what came earlier

rows.en: Farming began independently in at least eleven regions.
rows.html: Farming began independently in at least eleven regions.
rows.zh: 農業至少在十一個地區各自獨立地開始。
rows.note_en: independently: separately, without help from one another

rows.en: The change happened gradually, over thousands of years.
rows.html: The change happened gradually, over thousands of years.
rows.zh: 這個變化是在幾千年裡慢慢發生的。
rows.note_en: gradually, over …: slowly, through a long time
rows.note_zh: 在一段很長的時間裡慢慢地

rows.en: One reason may be that the climate became steadier.
rows.html: One reason may be that the climate became steadier.
rows.zh: 其中一個原因，可能是氣候變得比較穩定。
rows.note_en: one reason may be that: a possible cause, not a certain one
rows.note_zh: 一個可能的原因（不是確定的）

rows.en: As a result, more people could live in one place.
rows.html: As a result, more people could live in one place.
rows.zh: 結果，同一個地方可以住更多人。
rows.note_en: as a result: what happened because of it

rows.en: A good harvest led to a full granary.
rows.html: A good harvest led to a full granary.
rows.zh: 一次好收成帶來了裝滿的穀倉。
rows.note_en: led to: caused, over time

rows.en: Researchers do not agree on why farming began.
rows.html: Researchers do not agree on why farming began.
rows.zh: 農業為什麼開始，研究者的看法並不一致。
rows.note_en: do not agree on: have different opinions about
rows.note_zh: 對某件事有不同的看法

rows.en: Farming brought more food, but it also brought new risks.
rows.html: Farming brought more food, but it also brought new risks.
rows.zh: 農業帶來了更多食物，但也帶來了新的風險。
rows.note_en: but it also: adding the other side

taiwan_then.eyebrow: Taiwan at That Time · 那時候的台灣
taiwan_then.en: Millet and rice, five thousand years ago
taiwan_then.lead_en: The oldest evidence of farming found in Taiwan so far is about 5,000 years old, and it is a handful of burned grains.
taiwan_then.lead_zh: 台灣目前找到最早的農業證據，大約是五千年前的——那是一小把燒焦的穀粒。
taiwan_then.intro_en: In Lesson 1, the oldest culture known in Taiwan belonged to people who lived by gathering, fishing, and hunting. Thousands of years later a new way of life appears in the ground: pottery marked with cord patterns, and small settled villages. Archaeologists call it the Dapenkeng Culture, the earliest Neolithic culture found so far in Taiwan.
taiwan_then.intro_zh: 第一課講過，台灣目前所知最古老的文化，屬於靠採集、捕魚和打獵生活的人。幾千年之後，地層裡出現了一種新的生活方式：有繩紋的陶器，和定居的小型聚落。考古學家稱它為大坌坑文化，是台灣目前發現最早的新石器時代文化。

facts.en: At the Nanguanlidong site in the Tainan Science Park, archaeologists from Academia Sinica found charred rice together with two kinds of millet, broomcorn and foxtail. (The study that reports them writes the site name as Nan-kuan-li East.) The site dates from about 5,000 to 4,300 years ago. They are the oldest rice and millet known in Taiwan so far.
facts.zh: 在臺南科學園區的南關里東遺址，中央研究院的考古學家發現了碳化的稻米，以及兩種小米類的穀物：黍和粟。這處遺址的年代大約是距今 5,000 到 4,300 年。這是目前所知臺灣最早的稻米和小米。
facts.src: Tsang et al., Botanical Studies 58 (2017); 中央研究院歷史文物陳列館

facts.en: The National Museum of Prehistory explains that this Neolithic culture was brought in by another group of people from the southeastern coast of the mainland. Academia Sinica puts it more cautiously: it may have been a new culture brought by migrants from overseas.
facts.zh: 國立臺灣史前文化博物館的說明是：這個新石器時代文化，是「另一群人由中國大陸東南沿海帶入」的。中央研究院說得比較保留：它「可能應是由海外移民而來的新文化」。
facts.src: 國立臺灣史前文化博物館・考古學習網

facts.en: How old is the Dapenkeng Culture? The National Museum of Prehistory says from a little over 6,000 to 5,000 years ago. An older Academia Sinica page (2001) gives about 7,000 to 4,700 years ago. The study of the grains dates that one site to 5,000 to 4,300 years ago. Each is a careful estimate from different evidence.
facts.zh: 大坌坑文化有多古老？國立臺灣史前文化博物館說大約六千多年前到五千年前。中央研究院一個比較早的網頁（2001 年）說距今大約 7,000 到 4,700 年。研究那些穀粒的論文，把那一處遺址定在距今 5,000 到 4,300 年。每一個都是從不同的證據仔細估出來的。
facts.src: 中央研究院「臺灣的考古」

facts.en: Millet is not only a thing of the past. The National Museum of Prehistory notes that most of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples once had millet as their main food, and each developed its own ceremonies and culture around it. In some communities and schools, millet is gradually being planted again.
facts.zh: 小米不只是過去的東西。國立臺灣史前文化博物館指出，臺灣原住民族早期大多數以小米為主食，並各自發展出獨特的儀式與文化。現在有些部落和學校正逐漸重新種起小米。
facts.src: 國立臺灣史前文化博物館電子報第 424 期 (2020)

links.zh: 台灣歷史第一課：很久以前的事，我們怎麼知道？

links.zh: 台灣歷史第二課：幾千年前，誰住在台灣？

culture_cards.eyebrow: Stories Behind the Evidence · 證據背後的故事
culture_cards.title_en: Burned bread, a swamp garden, eel traps, and the first friend
culture_cards.title_zh: 燒焦的麵包、沼澤裡的菜圃、捕鰻魚的水道，和第一個朋友
culture_cards.lead_en: Four short stories that do not fit the simple tale of “first hunting, then farming.”
culture_cards.lead_zh: 四個小故事，都不合「先打獵、後種田」那個簡單的說法。

cards.body_en: In a fireplace inside a stone building in the Black Desert of Jordan, archaeologists found burned crumbs. Under the microscope they turned out to be the remains of flat, bread-like loaves, made from wild grain and roots by foragers at least 4,000 years before farming began in the region. People knew how to make bread long before they grew the wheat for it.
cards.body_zh: 在約旦黑沙漠一座石砌建築裡的火塘中，考古學家找到了燒焦的碎屑。放到顯微鏡下一看，原來是像麵包一樣的扁餅——採集狩獵者用野生的穀子和根莖做的，比當地開始有農業早了至少 4,000 年。人們早在種小麥之前，就已經會做麵包了。

cards.body_en: At Kuk, in the highlands of New Guinea, people heaped wet ground into mounds for planting about 7,000 years ago, and about 4,000 years ago began digging ditches to drain the swamp. UNESCO describes the site as wetland worked almost continuously for 7,000 years, and possibly for 10,000. The crops were bananas, taro, and yams, grown from cuttings and not from seed. The evidence suggests that farming developed there on its own, with no grain at all.
cards.body_zh: 在新幾內亞高地的庫克，人們大約 7,000 年前把濕地的土堆成一個個土丘來種東西，大約 4,000 年前開始挖溝把沼澤的水排掉。聯合國教科文組織形容這片濕地幾乎連續被人經營了 7,000 年，甚至可能有 10,000 年。這裡種的是香蕉、芋頭和薯蕷，用的是分株扦插，不是播種。證據顯示，農業在那裡是自己發展出來的——而且完全沒有穀類。

cards.zh: 另一種經營食物的方法
cards.body_en: At Budj Bim in southeastern Australia, the Gunditjmara people built channels, weirs, and dams in old lava flows to trap and keep eels. UNESCO says they created and reshaped this system over at least 6,600 years. They did not plant fields, yet they managed their own supply of food.
cards.body_zh: 在澳洲東南部的布吉必姆，貢第吉馬拉人（Gunditjmara）在古老的熔岩流上修築水道、堰和壩，用來捕捉和蓄養鰻魚。聯合國教科文組織說，他們建造並不斷改造這套系統，至少有 6,600 年。他們沒有種田，卻經營著自己的食物來源。

cards.body_en: The first animal people domesticated was not a farm animal. It was the dog, descended from wolves, living alongside hunters well before anyone farmed. When and where it happened is debated: one study argues for Siberia about 23,000 years ago.
cards.body_zh: 人類馴化的第一種動物不是農場上的牲畜。牠是狗，狼的後代，早在任何人開始種田之前就和獵人生活在一起了。這件事發生在什麼時候、什麼地方，還有爭論：有一項研究主張是大約 2.3 萬年前的西伯利亞。

curric.eyebrow: In the Curriculum · 對應課綱
curric.lead_en: These entries come from Taiwan's 12-Year Basic Education curriculum for social studies (October 2018). The curriculum has no entry on how farming began; the words for Neolithic and for domestication do not appear in it. This lesson is background for the entries below.
curric.lead_zh: 下面的條目出自十二年國民基本教育課程綱要社會領域（民國 107 年 10 月）。課綱裡沒有談「農業怎麼開始」的條目，整份文件也沒有出現「新石器」或「馴化」這些詞。這一課是下面這些條目的背景知識。

items.note_en: The “Taiwan at That Time” card presents the Dapenkeng Culture and the charred grains from the Tainan Science Park, and shows how the dates given by different institutions differ.
items.note_zh: 「那時候的台灣」介紹大坌坑文化和臺南科學園區出土的碳化穀粒，並且讓學生看到不同機構給的年代並不一樣。

items.area: 國中・古代文化的遺產
items.area_en: Junior high · the heritage of ancient cultures
items.text: 非洲與西亞的早期文化。
items.note_en: The early cultures of Egypt and Mesopotamia were built on farming. This lesson explains where that farming came from.
items.note_zh: 埃及和兩河流域的早期文化都建立在農業上。這一課說明那些農業是從哪裡來的。

items.note_en: The geography entry is about farming today. The map in this lesson shows the same link in the distant past: each region domesticated the plants that suited its own land.
items.note_zh: 地理的這一條談的是今天的農業。這一課的地圖讓學生看到，同樣的關聯在很久以前就有了：每個地區馴化的，都是適合當地土地的植物。

myths.myth_en: Farming was invented once, by one clever group, and everyone else copied them.
myths.myth_zh: 農業是某一群聰明人發明的，其他人都是跟他們學的。
myths.fact_en: Farming began independently in at least eleven regions, with different plants in each. Even inside West Asia, crops were domesticated slowly in several places, not in one “home” village.
myths.fact_zh: 農業至少在十一個地區各自獨立地開始，每個地區用的植物都不一樣。就算在西亞內部，作物也是在好幾個地方慢慢馴化的，並沒有一個「發源的村子」。

myths.myth_en: The Agricultural Revolution was a sudden event.
myths.myth_zh: 「農業革命」是突然發生的。
myths.fact_en: It was a slow change. For wheat, barley, and rice, it took about 2,000 to 4,000 years before the trait that keeps seeds on the stalk became fixed, and in many places people kept gathering and hunting throughout.
myths.fact_zh: 它是一個緩慢的變化。以小麥、大麥和稻來說，「種子留在穗上」這個特徵要花大約 2,000 到 4,000 年才固定下來；這段時間，許多地方的人也一直在採集和打獵。

myths.myth_en: Farmers were healthier and better fed than the hunter-gatherers before them.
myths.myth_zh: 農人比之前的採集狩獵者更健康、吃得更好。
myths.fact_en: In most of the places studied, people became shorter when they took up farming, and one survey found health declining in 19 of 21 societies. The number of people grew; their health, in most places studied, did not improve.
myths.fact_zh: 在大多數研究過的地方，人開始種田以後變矮了；有一項調查發現，21 個社會裡有 19 個的健康狀況變差。人數增加了；但在大多數研究過的地方，健康並沒有變好。

myths.myth_en: Hunter-gatherers were always on the move and always hungry.
myths.myth_zh: 採集狩獵的人總是在搬家，也總是在挨餓。
myths.fact_en: Some foragers lived in long-lasting settlements thousands of years before farming, and they baked bread from wild grain. Their lives were not easy, and they knew hunger too, but they were not simply waiting for farming to rescue them.
myths.fact_zh: 有些採集狩獵者在農業出現的幾千年前，就住在長期使用的聚落裡，還會用野生的穀子烤麵包。他們的日子並不輕鬆，也嘗過挨餓的滋味，但他們並不是在等農業來拯救自己。

tricks.body_en: Wheat, rice, millet, maize, bananas, sorghum: different plants, different places, the same idea.
tricks.body_zh: 小麥、稻、小米、玉米、香蕉、高粱：不同的植物、不同的地方、同一個點子。

tricks.body_en: Thousands of years, not one harvest. People planted long before the plants looked different.
tricks.body_zh: 是幾千年，不是一次收成。在植物看起來不一樣之前很久，人就已經在種了。

tricks.body_en: More food and more people, in exchange for more risk, more sickness, and a life tied more closely to one place.
tricks.body_zh: 更多食物、更多人，換來的是更多風險、更多疾病，和更離不開一個地方的生活。

tricks.title_en: Ask what went up and what went down
tricks.body_en: When someone says a change was “progress,” ask who gained, who lost, and how we know.
tricks.body_zh: 有人說某個改變是「進步」的時候，問一問：誰得到了好處？誰吃了虧？我們是怎麼知道的？

materials.en: About 100 dried beans of one color and 10 of another color (for example, 100 red beans and 10 mung beans)
materials.zh: 一種顏色的乾豆子大約 100 顆，另一種顏色的 10 顆（例如紅豆 100 顆、綠豆 10 顆）

materials.en: A tray, a cup, and a sheet for recording each round
materials.zh: 一個托盤、一個杯子、一張記錄每一回合的紙

steps.en: Spread all the beans on the tray. This is a field of wild grain. The many are plants that drop their seeds; the few are plants that hold on to them.
steps.zh: 把所有豆子攤在托盤上。這是一片野生的穀子。多的那一種是種子會自己掉落的植株，少的那一種是種子會留在穗上的。

steps.en: Harvest time. Tilt the tray so that about half of the many slide off: those seeds fell before you came. None of the few fall. Scoop what is left into the cup.
steps.zh: 收割的時候到了。把托盤斜一下，讓多的那一種大約滑掉一半——那些種子在你來之前就掉了。少的那一種一顆也不會掉。把剩下的都舀進杯子裡。

steps.en: Next year's field is sown from the cup. Count the two colors, then build a new field of 110 beans with the same proportions.
steps.zh: 明年的田是用杯子裡的種子播的。數一數兩種顏色各有多少，再照同樣的比例擺出一片 110 顆豆子的新田。

steps.en: Repeat for six rounds. In English, say what is happening each time: “The share of seeds that stay is going up, gradually.”
steps.zh: 重複六個回合。每一回合用英文說出發生了什麼事：「The share of seeds that stay is going up, gradually.」

activities.tip_en: Nobody in this game decides to change the plant. Ask the class: did the first farmers know what they were doing to the wheat? Real crops changed far more slowly than the beans, because people did not always harvest and sow in this way.
activities.tip_zh: 這個遊戲裡沒有任何人「決定」要改變植物。問問全班：最早的農人知道自己對小麥做了什麼嗎？真正的作物變得比豆子慢得多，因為人們並不是每一次都這樣收割和播種。

materials.en: The six cards from the “What Changed?” game, copied onto slips of paper
materials.zh: 「什麼變了？」遊戲裡的六張卡，抄在紙條上

materials.en: Two signs for opposite walls: “I would farm” and “I would keep gathering”
materials.zh: 兩張貼在對面牆上的牌子：「I would farm」和「I would keep gathering」

steps.en: Read out the valley from the model: a river, a wood, a meadow, good soil on one bank. Each student is the head of a family there.
steps.zh: 唸出模型裡的那座河谷：一條河、一片樹林、一片草地，其中一岸的土很肥。每位學生都是住在那裡的一家之主。

steps.en: Hand out the slips one at a time. After each one, students may walk toward one wall or the other, and one student explains the move in English.
steps.zh: 一次發一張紙條。每發一張，學生可以往其中一面牆走幾步，並且請一位學生用英文說明為什麼。

steps.en: Add a new situation: “Suppose the family across the river has started farming, and now there are many more of them.” Does anyone move?
steps.zh: 加一個新的情況：「假設河對岸那一家開始種田了，現在他們的人多了很多。」有人要移動嗎？

steps.en: Finish by writing one sentence each: “I would … because …, but I would worry about …”
steps.zh: 最後每人寫一句：「I would … because …, but I would worry about …」

activities.tip_en: There is no right wall. Step 3 matters most: once a neighbor farms, the choice may no longer be entirely free. Ask the class whether that could be one reason farming, once begun, was hard to give up.
activities.tip_zh: 沒有哪一面牆才是對的。第三步最重要：一旦鄰居開始種田，這個選擇可能就不再完全自由了。問問全班：這會不會是農業一旦開始就很難放棄的原因之一？

links.en: Why Did People Invent Writing?
links.zh: 人為什麼發明文字？
links.note_en: A full granary raises a new problem: whose grain is it, and how much is left? Lesson 3 follows the marks people made to keep count, and how they became writing.
links.note_zh: 裝滿的穀倉帶來一個新問題：這些穀子是誰的？還剩多少？第三課要看人們為了記帳而刻下的記號，後來怎麼變成了文字。

links.en: How Did Humans Spread Across the World?
links.zh: 人類怎麼走到世界各地？
links.note_en: By the time farming began, people already lived on every continent except Antarctica, so it could begin on several of them.
links.note_zh: 農業開始的時候，除了南極洲以外的每一洲都已經有人居住，所以它才能在好幾洲各自開始。

links.en: How Does a Seed Know When to Grow?
links.zh: 種子怎麼知道什麼時候該發芽？
links.note_en: What is inside a seed, and what it waits for. The first farmers learned this by watching.
links.note_zh: 種子裡面有什麼、它在等什麼。最早的農人是靠觀察學會這些的。

links.en: How Do We Know What Happened Long Ago?
links.zh: 很久以前的事，我們怎麼知道？
links.note_en: How layers in the ground are read, including the layers that hold Taiwan's first farmers.
links.note_zh: 地層是怎麼讀的——包括埋著台灣最早的農人的那些地層。

lessons.title: Why Did People Invent Writing?
lessons.blurb_en: Press number signs into a clay tablet in 3D, the way a scribe in ancient Mesopotamia kept accounts. Then find on a map the few places where writing began on its own, and discover the trick that let pictures write down names and speech.
lessons.blurb_zh: 在 3D 泥板上壓出數字記號，像古代美索不達米亞的書吏那樣記帳。再從地圖上找出文字各自開始的幾個地方，並發現讓圖畫能寫下名字和說話的那個訣竅。
lessons.big_idea_en: Writing was invented from scratch in only a few places. Its first uses were mostly practical: keeping accounts in Mesopotamia, asking questions of the spirits in China, recording dates in Mesoamerica. Over time, people learned to use signs for sounds, and writing could record anything people said.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 文字從無到有被發明出來的地方只有少數幾個。它最早的用途大多很實際：美索不達米亞拿來記帳，中國拿來向神靈提問，中部美洲拿來記日子。後來，人學會用記號代表聲音，文字就能記下人說的任何話。

lab.how_en: A scribe in ancient Mesopotamia needs to record how many sheep came in. Choose a number and press “Write it”: the reed stylus presses one mark at a time into the soft clay. Switch between the older number signs of the first tablets, pressed with a round-ended stylus, and the later Babylonian way, built from just two wedge-shaped signs. In the Babylonian way, try 1 and then 61, and look closely at what changes. The signs are simplified from museum and research descriptions; real tablets vary from scribe to scribe and century to century.
lab.how_zh: 古代美索不達米亞的一位書吏要記下進來了幾隻羊。選一個數字，按「寫上去」：蘆葦筆會一下一下把記號壓進軟軟的泥裡。可以切換兩種數字的寫法：最早的泥板上用圓頭的筆壓出來的數字記號，和後來巴比倫人只用兩種楔形記號組成的寫法。在巴比倫的寫法裡，先試 1，再試 61，仔細看看哪裡不一樣。記號的形狀是依博物館與研究的說明簡化的；真正的泥板，每位書吏、每個世紀都不完全一樣。
lab.wedge_zh: 後來：巴比倫的楔形數字

legend.en: Clay tablet: soft when written, hard once it dries
legend.zh: 泥板：寫的時候是軟的，乾了就變硬

legend.en: Reed stylus: a cut reed pressed into the clay
legend.zh: 蘆葦筆：削過的蘆葦，壓進泥裡

lab.scale_en: This is a teaching sketch. The number signs follow the general pattern described by museums and by the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative, but their exact shapes, sizes, and arrangement changed over three thousand years of use, and one model cannot show them all. Real accounts also named what was counted, with a word sign beside the number; that part is left out here rather than drawn from guesswork. The older signs shown are the ones used for counting things such as sheep and workers; grain and other goods had number systems of their own, and those older signs had no place value.
lab.scale_zh: 這是教學用的示意。數字記號依照博物館與「楔形文字數位圖書館計畫」（CDLI）描述的大致規則畫成，但它們確切的形狀、大小和排列方式，在三千年的使用裡一直在變，一個模型沒辦法全部呈現。真正的帳目還會在數字旁邊寫上一個代表「數的是什麼」的字；這一部分這裡省略了，不憑猜測去畫。模型裡比較早的那一種記號，是用來數羊、數工人這類東西的；穀物和其他貨物各有自己的計數系統，而且那時的記號還沒有位值。
lab.credit_html: Model: an illustration made for this lesson, after descriptions of cuneiform and proto-cuneiform number signs by the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative and museum collections listed in the sources. 模型：為這一課製作的示意，依「楔形文字數位圖書館計畫」與出處所列博物館對楔形文字、原始楔形文字數字記號的說明繪製。

paras: Think back to the granary in Lesson 2. A village has hundreds of sheep, many families, and a store of grain that has to last until the next harvest. Who brought how much? Who still owes some? Memory is not enough for questions like these. In the cities of southern Mesopotamia, people began to answer them with marks pressed into small pieces of soft clay.

The oldest known writing comes from the city of Uruk, about 3350 to 3000 BCE. A scribe pressed the end of a cut reed into wet clay, and the tablet hardened as it dried in the hot, dry air. Most of these early tablets are accounts: grain, animals, workers, and the food paid to them. A smaller number are lists of words, probably used to train scribes. Writing here began as a tool for keeping track of things.

Writing was not invented only once. Many scholars count four places where it began from scratch: Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, and Mesoamerica. In Egypt, labels from early royal tombs date from about the same time as the Uruk tablets. In China, the earliest surviving writing was carved on shells and bones more than 3,000 years ago, recording the Shang kings' questions and predictions about the future, addressed to their ancestors and spirits. In Mesoamerica, writing recorded dates in a calendar, and later the names and deeds of rulers.

A picture can show a sheep or a jar of grain, but how do you draw a name, or a word like “and”? The answer was a clever trick: use a picture for its sound. In English, a drawing of an eye could stand for the word “I.” Egyptian hieroglyphs used both kinds of signs, some for meanings and some for sounds. Most Chinese characters joined a part that hints at the meaning with a part that hints at the sound.

Perhaps as early as 1800 BCE, people who spoke a Semitic language took a few Egyptian signs and used each one for a single sound. Exactly where and when this happened is still argued over. This was the beginning of the alphabet, which later passed to the Phoenicians, the Greeks, and the Romans. An alphabet needs far fewer signs. But that does not make it better than other scripts. Chinese characters, Japanese kana, and many other systems serve the languages they write very well.

Writing changed what people could do. A promise, a law, or a list could now outlast the person who made it. For most of its history, though, writing was the skill of a few, such as trained scribes. Most people passed on their history by telling it. In Taiwan, the long age before written records is called prehistory. The National Museum of Prehistory names Chen Di's account of 1603 as the earliest record of Taiwan's customs; older Chinese texts may mention the island, but scholars disagree.
paras_zh: 回想第二課的穀倉。一個村子有好幾百隻羊、很多戶人家，還有一倉要吃到下一次收成的穀子。誰交了多少？誰還欠著？這種問題光靠記憶是不夠的。在美索不達米亞南部的城市裡，人們開始用壓在一小塊軟泥上的記號來回答這些問題。
已知最早的文字來自烏魯克城，大約是西元前 3350 到 3000 年。書吏把削過的蘆葦一端壓進濕泥裡，泥板在又熱又乾的空氣中乾了就變硬。這些早期的泥板大多是帳目：穀物、牲畜、工人，以及發給他們的食物。比較少的一部分是單字的清單，大概是用來訓練書吏的。在這裡，文字一開始是用來記住東西的工具。
文字不只被發明了一次。許多學者認為它從無到有出現在四個地方：美索不達米亞、埃及、中國和中部美洲。在埃及，早期王室墓葬裡的標籤和烏魯克的泥板差不多同一個時期。在中國，留存下來最早的文字刻在三千多年前的龜甲和獸骨上，記錄商王向祖先和神靈提出的、關於未來的問題與預測。在中部美洲，文字記下曆法上的日子，後來也記統治者的名字和事蹟。
圖畫可以畫出一隻羊、一甕穀子，可是名字要怎麼畫？像「和」這樣的字要怎麼畫？答案是一個很聰明的辦法：借用圖畫的聲音。在英文裡，畫一隻眼睛（eye）可以代表「我」（I）。埃及的聖書體兩種記號都用，有的代表意思，有的代表聲音。大多數的漢字，則是把提示意思的部分和提示聲音的部分合在一起。
可能早在西元前 1800 年，說閃語的人拿了幾個埃及的記號，讓每一個只代表一個聲音。這件事確切發生在哪裡、什麼時候，至今仍有爭論。這就是字母的開始，後來傳給了腓尼基人、希臘人和羅馬人。字母需要的記號少得多。但這並不表示它比別的文字好。漢字、日文的假名和許多其他的文字系統，都把它們所寫的語言服務得很好。
文字改變了人能做的事。一個承諾、一條法律、一份清單，現在可以比說出它的人留得更久。不過在文字歷史上大部分的時間裡，讀寫是少數人的技能，例如受過訓練的書吏。大多數的人是靠口耳相傳，把自己的歷史傳下去。在台灣，沒有文字記錄的漫長年代稱為史前時代。國立臺灣史前文化博物館指出，陳第 1603 年寫成的記述是最早關於台灣風俗的紀錄；更早的中文典籍可能提過這座島，但學者看法不一。
questions: What were the earliest tablets from Uruk mostly used for, and why does that make sense after Lesson 2?
Why couldn't early writers simply draw everything they wanted to say?
The lesson says an alphabet is not “better” than other writing systems. What reasons does it give?
answers: Mostly for accounts: grain, animals, workers, and the food paid to them. Lesson 2 showed that farming villages stored grain and kept herds, which raised questions of who owned what and who owed what. Those questions are hard to answer from memory alone.
Many things cannot be drawn: names, small words like “and” or “if,” and ideas. Using a picture for its sound let writers spell out any word, including names.

An alphabet uses fewer signs, but other scripts, such as Chinese characters and Japanese kana, also serve their languages well. How good a script is depends on the language it writes and the people who use it, not on the number of its signs.

vocab.ex: The scribe recorded how many sheep came in.
vocab.exzh: 書吏記下了進來了幾隻羊。

vocab.ex: The clay tablet is smaller than your hand.
vocab.exzh: 這塊泥板比你的手還小。

vocab.ex: A scribe spent years learning to write.
vocab.exzh: 一位書吏要花好幾年學寫字。

vocab.ex: This sign stands for the number ten.
vocab.exzh: 這個記號代表數字十。

vocab.ex: The dove is a symbol of peace.
vocab.exzh: 鴿子是和平的象徵。

vocab.ex: The English alphabet has 26 letters.
vocab.exzh: 英文字母共有 26 個。

vocab.ex: No one has managed to decipher the Indus signs.
vocab.exzh: 還沒有人能解讀印度河的記號。

vocab.ex: The temple kept careful accounts of its grain.
vocab.exzh: 神廟把穀物的帳目記得很仔細。

quiz.q: What were most of the earliest tablets from Uruk used for?
options: Keeping accounts of goods, animals, and workers

quiz.q: How many places do many scholars say invented writing from scratch?
What did early writers do to write names and other things that are hard to draw?
options: Used a picture for its sound
Drew a portrait of each person
Waited for the alphabet to be invented

quiz.q: What were the earliest Chinese writings mostly about?
options: The Shang kings' questions and predictions about the future

quiz.q: Why are the Indus signs still a mystery?
options: No one has been able to decipher them
It is less than a hundred years old

parts_head.eyebrow: Try It in the Model · 在模型裡試試

parts.text_en: Watch the stylus press a single sign. In later cuneiform, the cut end of the reed leaves a wedge-shaped dent. Writing here is pressing, not drawing a line.
parts.text_zh: 看筆壓出一個記號。在後來的楔形文字裡，削過的蘆葦一端會留下一個楔形的凹痕。這裡的「寫」是「壓」，不是畫線。

parts.text_en: Two signs worth ten and three worth one. A scribe could write a large count with only two kinds of mark, and anyone trained could read it back.
parts.text_zh: 兩個代表十的記號，加三個代表一的記號。書吏只用兩種記號就能寫出很大的數，受過訓練的人都讀得回來。

parts.text_en: The same number in the signs of the earliest tablets, pressed with a round-ended stylus. Different shapes, the same idea: a few signs, each worth a set amount.
parts.text_zh: 同一個數字，用最早的泥板上那種記號，由圓頭的筆壓出來。形狀不一樣，點子一樣：幾種記號，每一種代表一個固定的數量。

parts.text_en: In the Babylonian way, used from about 2000 BCE, 61 is written with two upright wedges, and the left one means sixty. Its place tells you its value, as the 1 in 10 means ten. There was no zero sign, so 1 and 60 on their own looked the same, and readers relied on the context.
parts.text_zh: 在大約西元前 2000 年起使用的巴比倫寫法裡，61 寫成兩個直楔，左邊那一個代表六十。它的位置決定它的值，就像 10 裡面的 1 代表十。那時沒有代表零的記號，所以單獨的 1 和 60 看起來一樣，要靠上下文判斷。

lessons.parts_note_en: Then pick your own number. Try 10 and 60 in the Babylonian way, and ask a friend to read your tablet without looking at the number.
lessons.parts_note_zh: 接著自己挑一個數字。在巴比倫的寫法裡試試 10 和 60，再請同學不看數字，讀讀看你的泥板。

centers.lead_en: Pull the slider from about 5,600 years ago toward the present. Each place lights up when its earliest known writing appears, faintly while the dates are uncertain and strongly once the evidence is clear. Click a number to see what the first writing there was used for.
centers.lead_zh: 把滑桿從大約 5,600 年前往現在拉。每個地方在出現已知最早的文字時亮起來：年代還不確定的時候淡淡的，證據明確了才變實。點一個號碼，看看那裡最早的文字是拿來做什麼的。
centers.count_zh: 目前已經有文字的地方
centers.idle_en: Click a numbered circle on the map, or a name below it.
centers.idle_zh: 點地圖上有號碼的圓，或是地圖下面的名字。
centers.foot_en: Many scholars count four places where writing was invented from scratch: Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, and Mesoamerica. Whether Egypt's writing owed anything to Mesopotamia's is still discussed. The signs of the Indus Valley are shown too, but they have not been deciphered, and whether they record a language is debated.
centers.foot_zh: 許多學者認為文字從無到有被發明了四次：美索不達米亞、埃及、中國和中部美洲。埃及的文字有沒有受到美索不達米亞的影響，至今仍在討論。印度河流域的記號也畫在地圖上，但它們還沒有被解讀，是不是在記錄一種語言也有爭論。

centers.crops_en: Mostly accounts: grain, animals, workers, and the rations paid to them. Also lists of words, probably used to train scribes.
centers.crops_zh: 大多是帳目：穀物、牲畜、工人，以及發給他們的口糧。也有一些單字的清單，大概是拿來訓練書吏的。
centers.when_en: About 3350 to 3000 BCE, on clay tablets from the city of Uruk.
centers.when_zh: 大約西元前 3350 到 3000 年，出自烏魯克城的泥板。
centers.note_en: This writing grew into cuneiform, which was used for more than three thousand years.
centers.note_zh: 這種文字後來發展成楔形文字，用了三千多年。
centers.src: Everson and Hawkins, proto-cuneiform proposal to Unicode (2016)

centers.crops_en: Small labels of bone and ivory from early royal tombs, thought to give goods, quantities, places, and people's names.
centers.crops_zh: 早期王室墓葬裡用骨頭和象牙做的小標籤，一般認為記的是貨物、數量、地名和人名。
centers.when_en: About 3320 BCE according to a University of Chicago exhibition; another study places them at about 3300 to 3100 BCE.
centers.when_zh: 依芝加哥大學一場展覽的說法大約是西元前 3320 年；另一項研究把它們放在大約西元前 3300 到 3100 年。
centers.note_en: Much of what they say is worked out from later Egyptian writing. Egyptian hieroglyphs grew from this beginning.
centers.note_zh: 它們寫了什麼，很多是靠後來的埃及文字推敲出來的。埃及的聖書體就是從這裡發展出來的。
centers.src: University of Chicago News (2010); Piquette, in Writing as Material Practice (2013)

centers.crops_en: Short groups of signs, mostly on small stone seals. No one can read them yet.
centers.crops_zh: 一小串一小串的記號，大多刻在小小的石頭印章上。至今還沒有人讀得懂。
centers.when_en: The civilization that used them flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE.
centers.when_zh: 使用它們的文明，大約從西元前 2600 年興盛到 1900 年。
centers.note_en: Some researchers argue that these signs are not writing at all; others answer that their patterns look like those of a language.
centers.note_zh: 有研究者主張這些記號根本不是文字；也有研究者回應，它們的規律看起來像是一種語言。
centers.src: Rao et al., Science (2009); Farmer, Sproat, and Witzel (2004)

centers.crops_en: Questions, predictions, and requests addressed by the Shang kings to their ancestors and spirits, carved on turtle shells and cattle bones.
centers.crops_zh: 商王對祖先和神靈的提問、預測和祈求，刻在龜甲和牛骨上。
centers.when_en: More than 3,000 years ago, at Anyang, the Shang capital of that time. One museum source puts the start at about 1200 BCE.
centers.when_zh: 三千多年前，在當時商朝的都城安陽。有一份博物館資料把開始的時間定在大約西元前 1200 年。
centers.note_en: Lesson 5 of the Chinese Calligraphy series tells how these characters changed over the centuries.
centers.note_zh: 書法系列第五課講這些字後來幾千年怎麼變。
centers.src: University of Chicago Magazine (2011); Penn Museum, Expedition (1989)

centers.crops_en: One of the earliest Maya texts includes a date in a ritual calendar.
centers.crops_zh: 最早的馬雅文字之一，記有一個儀式曆法上的日子。
centers.when_en: A stone block found in Mexico was dated by its finders to the early first millennium BCE; it is the only text of its kind, and other scholars question it. Maya writing at San Bartolo is from about 300 to 200 BCE.
centers.when_zh: 在墨西哥發現的一塊石頭，發現者把它定在西元前第一個千年早期；它是同類中唯一的一件，也有學者對它有疑問。聖巴托洛的馬雅文字大約是西元前 300 到 200 年的。
centers.note_en: The San Bartolo fragment includes the oldest dated Maya calendar sign found so far, a day called “7 Deer.”
centers.note_zh: 聖巴托洛的這片殘片裡，有目前所知最早、可以定年的馬雅曆法記號——一個叫做「七鹿」的日子。
centers.src: Stuart et al., Science Advances (2022); Rodríguez Martínez et al., Science (2006)

signs.lead_en: Pictures can show things, but they cannot easily show names or small words. Early writers solved this with a trick: they used a picture for its sound. These examples use English words. For each one, decide whether the picture means the thing it shows, or stands for a sound. There is no timer.
signs.lead_zh: 圖畫可以畫出東西，卻很難畫出名字或小小的虛字。早期的書寫者想出了一個辦法：借用一個圖畫的「聲音」。下面的例子用的是英文字。每一題判斷：這個圖畫的是它本來的東西，還是借它的聲音？不計時。
signs.ask_en: What is the picture doing here?

items.en: 👁️ written to mean “an eye”
items.why_en: The picture means exactly what it shows.
items.why_zh: 圖畫的意思就是它畫的東西。
items.hint_en: Is the meaning the same as the picture?
items.hint_zh: 意思和圖畫的是不是同一個東西？

items.en: 👁️ written to mean the word “I”
items.why_en: “Eye” and “I” sound the same in English, so the picture borrows the sound. A University of Chicago article uses this very example to explain how Egyptian writing worked.
items.why_zh: 英文的 eye 和 I 唸起來一樣，所以借用了圖畫的聲音。芝加哥大學的一篇文章就是用這個例子，說明埃及文字的原理。
items.hint_en: Say the word out loud.
items.hint_zh: 把字唸出來聽聽看。

items.en: 🐑🐑🐑 written to mean “three sheep”
items.why_en: Counting things is what pictures and number signs do well, which is one reason the earliest accounts could be kept this way.
items.why_zh: 數東西正是圖畫和數字記號擅長的事，這也是最早的帳目能這樣記下來的原因之一。
items.hint_en: Is anything being said about a sound?
items.hint_zh: 這裡有沒有用到任何聲音？

items.en: 🐝 + 🍃 written to mean “belief”
items.why_en: A bee and a leaf have nothing to do with belief. Put their sounds together, “bee-leaf,” and you get the word.
items.why_zh: 蜜蜂和葉子跟「信念」毫無關係。把兩個聲音接起來 bee-leaf，就是那個字。
items.hint_en: A belief is not an insect.
items.hint_zh: 信念不是一種昆蟲。

items.en: ☀️ written to mean “the sun”
items.why_en: The picture shows the thing.
items.why_zh: 圖畫的就是那個東西。
items.hint_en: Look up at the sky.
items.hint_zh: 抬頭看看天空。

items.en: ☀️ written in “My ☀️ is ten years old”
items.zh: ☀️ 寫在「My ☀️ is ten years old.」這一句裡
items.why_en: The sun is not ten years old. Here the picture stands for the sound of “son.”
items.why_zh: 太陽不會只有十歲。這裡的圖借的是 son（兒子）的聲音。
items.hint_en: Who could be ten years old?
items.hint_zh: 誰才可能是十歲？

items.en: 🔑 written as part of the name “Lu-🔑” (Luke)
items.why_en: Names are the hardest thing to draw. Borrowing the sound of “key” lets you write a name that has no picture.
items.why_zh: 名字是最難畫的東西。借用 key 的聲音，就能寫出一個畫不出來的名字。
items.hint_en: Can you draw a picture of a name?
items.hint_zh: 名字畫得出來嗎？

items.en: 🔑 written in “Lock the door and keep the 🔑”
items.zh: 🔑 寫在「Lock the door and keep the 🔑.」這一句裡
items.why_en: Here the key really is a key.
items.why_zh: 這裡的鑰匙，真的就是鑰匙。
items.hint_en: What do you lock a door with?
items.hint_zh: 鎖門用的是什麼？

signs.end_en: Using pictures for their sounds was a turning point. Once signs could stand for sounds, people could write names, small words, and in time anything they could say.
signs.end_zh: 借用圖畫的聲音是一個轉折點。一旦記號可以代表聲音，人就能寫下名字、小小的虛字，最後是任何說得出口的話。

timeline.zh: 文字一條線一條線地出現
timeline.lead_en: Each bar marks the earliest known writing in a region. Notice how far apart they are, and how much of human history lies to the left of all of them. Press “Whole span” to see it.
timeline.lead_zh: 每一條長條標出一個地區已知最早的文字。注意它們彼此隔得多遠，以及人類的歷史有多少是在它們全部的左邊。按「全部」看看。
timeline.idle_en: Click a bar or a diamond to read its dates.
timeline.idle_zh: 點一條長條或一個菱形，讀出它的年代。

tips.en: Bars that are far apart and in different lanes are the strongest sign that writing was invented more than once.
tips.zh: 相隔很遠、又在不同線上的長條，是「文字不只被發明一次」最有力的證據。

tips.en: A striped bar marks a date, or a kind of evidence, that researchers still debate.
tips.zh: 有條紋的長條，是研究者還在爭論的年代或證據。

tips.en: The gray diamonds mark a beginning and an ending: the first alphabet, and the last known cuneiform tablet.
tips.zh: 灰色的菱形標的是一個開始和一個結束：最早的字母，以及已知最後一塊楔形文字泥板。

events.note_en: Clay tablets, most of them accounts.
events.note_zh: 泥板，大多是帳目。

events.note_en: About the same time as Uruk; dates range from about 3320 to 3100 BCE in different sources.
events.note_zh: 和烏魯克差不多同時；不同資料的年代從大約西元前 3320 到 3100 年。

events.note_en: Whether these signs record a language is debated.
events.note_zh: 這些記號是不是在記錄語言，還有爭論。

events.note_en: Signs borrowed from Egyptian hieroglyphs, each used for one sound, possibly as early as 1800 BCE.
events.note_zh: 借用埃及聖書體的記號，每一個只代表一個聲音，可能早在西元前 1800 年。

events.note_en: Questions and predictions addressed to ancestors and spirits, carved on shell and bone more than 3,000 years ago. One museum source puts the start of Chinese writing at about 1200 BCE.
events.note_zh: 刻在龜甲和獸骨上、向祖先和神靈提出的問題與預測，距今三千多年。有一份博物館資料把中國文字的開始定在大約西元前 1200 年。

events.note_en: The earliest Greek alphabetic inscriptions date to the 700s BCE.
events.note_zh: 最早的希臘字母銘文是西元前 700 年代的。

events.note_en: A disputed stone block from early in the first millennium BCE; Maya writing at San Bartolo about 300 to 200 BCE.
events.note_zh: 一塊有爭議、可能是西元前第一個千年早期的石塊；聖巴托洛的馬雅文字大約是西元前 300 到 200 年。

events.zh: 已知最後一塊楔形文字泥板
events.note_en: An astronomical text from 79 or 80 CE, more than 3,000 years after the first tablets.
events.note_zh: 一份天文記錄，年代是西元 79 或 80 年，距離最早的泥板三千多年。

how_we_know.eyebrow: How Do We Know? · 我們怎麼知道？
how_we_know.en: What survived, and how it was read
how_we_know.zh: 留下來的東西，以及怎麼讀懂它
how_we_know.lead_en: With writing, the evidence finally speaks for itself, but only if it has survived and only if someone can read it.
how_we_know.lead_zh: 有了文字，證據終於能自己說話——但前提是它留了下來，而且有人讀得懂。

items.en: Clay that lasts
items.limit_en: Writing on papyrus, wood, bamboo, cloth, or leaves rots away, so what survives is not all that was written. A place with few surviving texts may simply have written on softer things.
items.limit_zh: 寫在莎草紙、木頭、竹子、布或葉子上的字會腐爛，所以留下來的並不是當時寫的全部。一個留下很少文字的地方，可能只是寫在比較不耐久的東西上。
items.src: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative; Penn Museum, Expedition (1976)
items.text_en: Most clay tablets were only dried in the sun, yet in the dry climate of Mesopotamia a great many survived in the ground. More than half a million are now kept in collections around the world.
items.text_zh: 大多數的泥板只是曬乾而已，但在美索不達米亞乾燥的氣候裡，很多都在地底下保存了下來。現在世界各地的收藏裡有超過五十萬塊。

items.en: Shells and bones
items.limit_en: Almost all of them are records of the royal court asking about the future. They tell us little about how ordinary people lived or spoke.
items.limit_zh: 它們幾乎都是王室向未來提問的記錄，對一般人怎麼生活、怎麼說話，說得很少。
items.src: 教育部 教育百科「甲骨文」
items.text_en: The Shang kings' questions and predictions were carved on turtle shells and cattle bones and buried at Anyang. They were recognized as writing in 1899 and have been dug up in great numbers since.
items.text_zh: 商王的提問和預測刻在龜甲和牛骨上，埋在安陽。它們在 1899 年被認出是文字，之後大量出土。

items.en: Reading a lost script
items.limit_en: Some scripts have never been deciphered, such as the Indus signs. Without a key, or a language we know, the marks stay silent.
items.limit_zh: 有些文字至今沒有被解讀，例如印度河的記號。沒有鑰匙，也不知道它記的是哪一種語言，這些記號就一直沉默。
items.src: University of Cambridge, Faculty of Classics, “The Life of Michael Ventris”
items.text_en: When a script stops being used, it has to be deciphered. Michael Ventris announced his decipherment of the Greek script called Linear B in 1952, and in the same year the Russian scholar Yuri Knorozov announced that he could match some Maya signs to Maya words.
items.text_zh: 一種文字不再有人使用之後，就得重新「解讀」。1952 年，文屈斯（Michael Ventris）宣布解讀了一種叫「線形文字 B」的希臘文字；同一年，俄國學者克諾羅佐夫（Yuri Knorozov）宣布他能把一些馬雅的記號和馬雅語的字對起來。

views.en: Four questions about the first writing
views.zh: 關於最早的文字的四個問題
views.lead_en: Even the beginning of writing, the point where history is said to start, is argued over. Here are four questions. The views are set side by side; this lesson does not choose between them.
views.lead_zh: 就連文字的開端——常被說是「歷史開始」的地方——也有爭論。下面是四個問題。各種說法並列，這一課不替誰下結論。
views.rule_en: Notice that the disagreements are not only about dates. They are also about definitions: what counts as writing at all.
views.rule_zh: 留意這些分歧不只是年代的問題，也是定義的問題：怎樣才算是「文字」？

items.topic_en: Was writing invented once, or several times?
items.topic_zh: 文字是被發明一次，還是好幾次？

sides.en: A curator at the University of Chicago's museum, describing the scholarship of the last few decades, counts four places where writing was invented from scratch: Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, and Mesoamerica.
sides.zh: 芝加哥大學博物館的一位策展人整理近幾十年的研究，認為文字在四個地方從無到有地被發明：美索不達米亞、埃及、中國和中部美洲。
sides.src: University of Chicago News (2010); University of Chicago Magazine (2011)

sides.en: An older view held that writing began in Mesopotamia and the idea spread from there. Egypt is still the case most debated, because its writing appeared at almost the same time, not far away.
sides.zh: 比較早的看法認為文字從美索不達米亞開始，這個點子再從那裡傳開。至今爭論最多的還是埃及，因為它的文字幾乎同時出現，距離又不遠。
sides.src: University of Chicago Magazine (2011)

items.note_en: Most scholars think Chinese and Mesoamerican writing began independently, although a few have argued that the idea of writing reached China from the west. The liveliest debate is about Egypt.
items.note_zh: 多數學者認為中國和中部美洲的文字是各自開始的，不過也有少數學者主張，「文字」這個點子是從西方傳到中國的。爭論最熱烈的是埃及。

items.topic_en: Did writing grow out of small clay tokens?
items.topic_zh: 文字是從小小的陶籌演變來的嗎？

sides.en: The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat argues that small clay tokens, used for counting goods from about 8000 to 3500 BCE, were the forerunners of the first written signs.
sides.zh: 考古學家施曼特－貝瑟拉（Denise Schmandt-Besserat）主張，大約西元前 8000 到 3500 年用來計算貨物的小陶籌，是最早的文字記號的前身。
sides.src: Schmandt-Besserat, “The Evolution of Writing,” University of Texas

sides.en: Reviewers have criticized her methods and pointed out that the tokens are too varied, and found over too wide an area, to fit one neat story. Other specialists accept that some simple tokens were forerunners of writing, but not all of her readings.
sides.zh: 書評者批評她的研究方法，並指出這些陶籌種類太多、分布太廣，放不進一個整齊的故事裡。也有專家接受其中一部分簡單的陶籌是文字的前身，但不接受她全部的解讀。
sides.src: Zimansky (1993); Michalowski (1993); Englund (c. 2011)

items.note_en: The theory has been partly accepted, not simply proved or disproved.
items.note_zh: 這個理論部分被接受，並沒有被簡單地證明或推翻。

items.topic_en: Are the Indus signs writing?
items.topic_zh: 印度河的記號是文字嗎？

sides.en: Three scholars argued in 2004 that the Indus signs were a system of symbols that did not record a spoken language.
sides.zh: 三位學者在 2004 年主張，印度河的記號是一套符號系統，並沒有記錄口說的語言。
sides.src: Farmer, Sproat, and Witzel, Electronic Journal of Vedic Studies 11 (2004)

sides.en: A 2009 study measured how the signs follow one another and found the patterns closer to those of languages than of non-linguistic systems.
sides.zh: 2009 年的一項研究測量記號前後相接的規律，發現它比較像語言，而不像非語言的符號系統。
sides.src: Rao et al., Science 324 (2009); a reply: Sproat, Computational Linguistics 36 (2010)

items.note_en: Until the signs are deciphered, if they ever are, the question stays open.
items.note_zh: 在這些記號被解讀之前（如果有那一天），這個問題都不會有答案。

items.topic_en: Was writing invented for keeping accounts?
items.topic_zh: 文字是為了記帳而發明的嗎？

sides.label_zh: 在美索不達米亞，大致是
sides.en: About 85 percent of the early tablets from Uruk are administrative records, by one specialist's count. He puts it plainly: cuneiform began with number signs.
sides.zh: 依一位專家的統計，烏魯克早期的泥板大約百分之八十五是行政記錄。他說得很直接：楔形文字是從數字記號開始的。
sides.src: Englund, “Accounting in Proto-cuneiform” (c. 2011)

sides.en: The earliest Chinese writing records divination, and one of the earliest Maya texts includes a calendar date. Even in Mesopotamia, word lists appear from the start, and one specialist suggests they may be the earliest known literature.
sides.zh: 中國最早的文字記的是占卜；最早的馬雅文字裡，有一段記的是曆法上的日子。就算在美索不達米亞，單字的清單也是一開始就有，有一位專家認為它們可能是已知最早的文學。
sides.src: University of Chicago Magazine (2011); Stuart et al. (2022)

items.note_en: “Why writing began” may have a different answer in each place it began.
items.note_zh: 「文字為什麼開始」，在每一個它開始的地方，答案可能都不一樣。

phrases.en: Eight sentences for talking about old writing
phrases.zh: 談古老文字的八句英文
phrases.lead_en: These sentences help you talk about writing the way historians do: what is the earliest known, what a sign stands for, and what is still unread. Listen, repeat, then make your own sentence with the words in bold.
phrases.lead_zh: 這八句幫你用歷史學家的方式談文字：已知最早的是什麼、一個記號代表什麼、什麼還沒有被讀懂。先聽、再跟著唸，然後用粗體的字自己造一句。

rows.en: The earliest known writing comes from Uruk.
rows.html: The earliest known writing comes from Uruk.
rows.zh: 已知最早的文字來自烏魯克。
rows.note_en: the earliest known: the oldest found so far

rows.en: Most of the first tablets were used to keep accounts.
rows.html: Most of the first tablets were used to keep accounts.
rows.zh: 最早的泥板大多是拿來記帳的。
rows.note_en: were used to + verb: what something was for

rows.en: This sign stands for the number ten.
rows.html: This sign stands for the number ten.
rows.zh: 這個記號代表數字十。
rows.note_en: stands for: means, represents

rows.en: A picture can stand for a sound as well as a thing.
rows.html: A picture can stand for a sound as well as a thing.
rows.zh: 一個圖畫可以代表一個聲音，也可以代表一個東西。
rows.note_en: stand for a sound: be used for how it is said

rows.en: The Indus signs have not been deciphered.
rows.html: The Indus signs have not been deciphered.
rows.zh: 印度河的記號還沒有被解讀。
rows.note_en: have not been deciphered: no one can read them yet

rows.en: Writing was invented independently in several places.
rows.html: Writing was invented independently in several places.
rows.zh: 文字在好幾個地方被各自獨立地發明。
rows.note_en: was invented independently: began separately

rows.en: Scholars generally agree that China invented its own writing.
rows.html: Scholars generally agree that China invented its own writing.
rows.zh: 學者一般都同意，中國的文字是自己發明的。
rows.note_en: scholars generally agree that: most experts think

rows.en: Writing made it possible to keep a promise after the speaker was gone.
rows.html: Writing made it possible to keep a promise after the speaker was gone.
rows.zh: 文字讓一個承諾在說話的人離開之後還能留下來。
rows.note_en: made it possible to: allowed something new

taiwan_then.eyebrow: Taiwan at That Time · 那時候的台灣
taiwan_then.en: From spoken history to written records
taiwan_then.zh: 從口傳的歷史到文字的記錄
taiwan_then.lead_en: When the first tablets were being pressed at Uruk, Taiwan's people were living through the age the museum calls prehistory. Their history was carried in memory and speech.
taiwan_then.lead_zh: 烏魯克的第一批泥板被壓出來的時候，台灣的住民正生活在博物館所說的史前時代。他們的歷史，是靠記憶和口語傳下來的。
taiwan_then.intro_en: History does not begin with writing; only written records do. Taiwan's story shows how much was passed on by speaking, and how writing arrived late, from outside, and was then taken up by the people themselves.
taiwan_then.intro_zh: 歷史不是從文字開始的，開始的只是文字的記錄。台灣的故事讓我們看到，有多少東西是靠說話傳下來的；也看到文字是很晚才從外面來的，後來又被這裡的人拿來自己用。

facts.en: The National Museum of Prehistory explains that prehistory is the age without written records, when people passed down what had happened by telling it, from one generation to the next.
facts.zh: 國立臺灣史前文化博物館說明：「史前時期是指沒有文字紀錄的年代，史前人們用口語流傳的方式，把過去發生的事一代傳一代地說給後代子孫聽。」
facts.src: 國立臺灣史前文化博物館「從史前走進歷史」

facts.en: In 1603 Chen Di wrote Dongfan ji, which the same museum calls the earliest record of customs in Taiwan. An older Chinese history, the Book of Sui, describes a place called Liuqiu, but scholars have long disagreed about whether it means Taiwan.
facts.zh: 1603 年，陳第寫下《東番記》，同一座博物館稱它留下了「最早關於臺灣風俗的紀錄」。更早的《隋書》描寫過一個叫「流求」的地方，但它指的是不是台灣，學者之間一直有不同的看法。
facts.src: 林鶴亭〈隋書流求傳之研究〉，《臺南文化》(1959)

facts.k_en: A language written in Latin letters
facts.en: In the 17th century Dutch missionaries taught Siraya communities to write their own language in Latin letters. The so-called Sinckan (or Sinkang) manuscripts, mostly land contracts and loans, kept being written long after the Dutch left: the earliest known is from 1683 and the latest from 1813 or 1818, depending on the source. More than 140 survive.
facts.zh: 十七世紀，荷蘭傳教士教西拉雅族的社群用羅馬字書寫自己的語言。所謂的「新港文書」大多是土地契約，荷蘭人離開以後還繼續有人寫：已知最早的是 1683 年，最晚的是 1813 年或 1818 年（兩份資料不同）。現存大約一百四十多件。
facts.src: 中央研究院民族學研究所〈新港文書〉；中央研究院臺灣史研究所檔案館

facts.en: Since 2005, Taiwan's Indigenous languages have had official writing systems in Latin letters, set by the Council of Indigenous Peoples and the Ministry of Education. The announcement itself names the Sinckan manuscripts as part of that history.
facts.zh: 2005 年起，臺灣的原住民族語言有了由原住民族委員會和教育部公告、以羅馬字書寫的書寫系統。公告本身就提到，「新港文書」是這段歷史的一部分。
facts.src: 原住民族委員會、教育部《原住民族語言書寫系統》(2005)

links.en: Taiwan's Story, Lesson 1: How Do We Know What Happened Long Ago?
links.zh: 台灣歷史第一課：很久以前的事，我們怎麼知道？

links.en: Taiwan's Story, Lesson 2: Who Lived in Taiwan Thousands of Years Ago?
links.zh: 台灣歷史第二課：幾千年前，誰住在台灣？

culture_cards.eyebrow: Stories Behind the Evidence · 證據背後的故事
culture_cards.title_en: A last tablet, an architect, a deer, and some old bones
culture_cards.title_zh: 最後一塊泥板、一位建築師、一隻鹿，和幾塊舊骨頭
culture_cards.lead_en: Four short stories about how writing ended, and how it was found again.
culture_cards.lead_zh: 四個小故事：文字怎麼結束，又怎麼被重新找到。

cards.k: 79 or 80 CE · Mesopotamia · 美索不達米亞
cards.body_en: Cuneiform was written for more than three thousand years. The latest datable tablet found so far is an astronomical text from 79 or 80 CE. After that, the script was forgotten until scholars in the 19th century learned to read it again.
cards.body_zh: 楔形文字被使用了三千多年。目前找到最晚、可以定年的一塊泥板，是西元 79 或 80 年的天文記錄。在那之後，這種文字被遺忘了，直到十九世紀的學者才又重新學會讀它。

cards.body_en: Clay tablets from ancient Crete and mainland Greece were written in a script called Linear B. For decades no one could read them. Michael Ventris, an architect, showed that they recorded an early form of Greek, and his decipherment was broadcast to the world on July 1, 1952.
cards.body_zh: 古代克里特島和希臘本土出土的泥板，寫的是一種叫「線形文字 B」的文字。幾十年來沒有人讀得懂。建築師文屈斯證明它記的是一種早期的希臘語，他的解讀在 1952 年 7 月 1 日透過廣播公諸於世。

cards.k: About 300–200 BCE · Mesoamerica · 中部美洲
cards.body_en: At San Bartolo in Guatemala, painted fragments of a wall carry the oldest dated Maya calendar sign found so far: a day called 7 Deer, in a 260-day calendar. It shows that keeping track of time was already part of the earliest Maya writing.
cards.body_zh: 在瓜地馬拉的聖巴托洛，一面牆的彩繪殘片上，有目前所知最早、可以定年的馬雅曆法記號：260 天曆法裡一個叫「七鹿」的日子。這說明記錄時間在最早的馬雅文字裡就已經出現了。

cards.body_en: Shells and bones from Xiaotun village near Anyang were recognized as ancient writing in 1899. One standard reference lists 4,672 different characters on them, of which 1,723 can be transcribed into later standard characters; the meanings of many are still unclear. Lesson 5 of the Chinese Calligraphy series looks at them closely.
cards.body_zh: 1899 年，安陽小屯村一帶出土的龜甲和獸骨被認出是古代的文字。一部常用的工具書收錄了上面 4,672 個不同的字，其中 1,723 個可以隸定成後來的楷字；很多字的意思到現在還不清楚。書法系列第五課會仔細看它們。

curric.eyebrow: In the Curriculum · 對應課綱
curric.lead_en: These entries come from Taiwan's 12-Year Basic Education curriculum for social studies (October 2018). The curriculum has no entry on the invention of writing. This lesson is enrichment for the entries below.
curric.lead_zh: 下面的條目出自十二年國民基本教育課程綱要社會領域（民國 107 年 10 月）。課綱裡沒有談「文字的發明」的條目。這一課是下面這些條目的延伸。

items.area: 國中・古代文化的遺產
items.area_en: Junior high · the heritage of ancient cultures
items.text: 非洲與西亞的早期文化。
items.note_en: The curriculum's explanation suggests focusing on Egypt and, in West Asia, on Sumer, Babylon, and Persia. This lesson shows the writing that those cultures left behind.
items.note_zh: 課綱的說明建議以埃及，以及西亞的蘇美、巴比倫和波斯為主。這一課讓學生看到這些文化留下的文字。

items.note_en: The curriculum's explanation notes that Taiwan's earliest inhabitants left no written records, so archaeology and oral tradition are the two main ways to trace them. The “Taiwan at That Time” card follows this line of thought.
items.note_zh: 課綱的說明寫道：「臺灣最早的主人們沒有留下文字資料，要追索他們在臺灣的足跡，考古資料和口頭傳說是最重要的兩個途徑。」「那時候的台灣」這張卡就是順著這個思路寫的。

myths.myth_en: Writing was invented to record stories, poems, and history.
myths.myth_zh: 文字是為了記錄故事、詩和歷史而發明的。
myths.fact_en: About 85 percent of the early tablets from Uruk are administrative records; in China the earliest writing records divination. Stories and poems came later, although word lists appear from the very start.
myths.fact_zh: 烏魯克早期的泥板大約百分之八十五是行政記錄；在中國，最早的文字記的是占卜。故事和詩是後來的事，不過單字的清單從一開始就有了。

myths.myth_en: Egyptian hieroglyphs are just pictures.
myths.myth_zh: 埃及的聖書體就只是圖畫。
myths.fact_en: They mixed picture signs with signs that stood for sounds, using the same trick as a picture of an eye standing for the word “I.”
myths.fact_zh: 它們把圖畫記號和代表聲音的記號混在一起用，用的就是「畫一隻眼睛代表 I」那種辦法。

myths.myth_en: Chinese characters are pictures of things.
myths.myth_zh: 漢字都是畫東西的圖。
myths.fact_en: A few began as pictures, but about nine in ten of the characters in the Shuowen jiezi, a dictionary from about 2,000 years ago, combine a meaning part with a sound part. In the much older oracle bone script, such characters were still a small share, perhaps 10 to 20 percent by one estimate.
myths.fact_zh: 有一些字一開始是圖畫，但在大約兩千年前的字典《說文解字》裡，大約十個字有九個是把表意的部分和表音的部分合在一起的形聲字。在更古老的甲骨文裡，這種字還只占一小部分，有一種估計是百分之十到二十左右。

myths.myth_en: The alphabet is the most advanced kind of writing.
myths.myth_zh: 字母是最先進的文字。
myths.fact_en: An alphabet uses fewer signs, but a museum essay on its history notes that widespread literacy does not require an alphabet. Many historians of writing would add that each script suits the language it was made for, so none is simply better than another.
myths.fact_zh: 字母用的記號比較少，但一篇談字母歷史的博物館文章指出，要讓很多人識字，並不一定需要字母。許多研究文字史的學者也會補充：每一種文字都適合它所寫的語言，所以沒有哪一種是單純比較好的。

tricks.title_en: First the count, then the story
tricks.body_en: In Mesopotamia, writing began with numbers and lists. Literature came much later.
tricks.body_zh: 在美索不達米亞，文字是從數字和清單開始的。文學是很久以後的事。

tricks.body_en: Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica. Different places, different signs, the same idea.
tricks.body_zh: 美索不達米亞、埃及、中國、中部美洲。不同的地方、不同的記號、同一個點子。

tricks.body_en: Eye for “I.” When a picture can stand for a sound, anything that can be said can be written.
tricks.body_zh: 用 eye 寫 I。一旦圖畫能代表聲音，說得出口的話就都寫得下來。

tricks.body_en: Alphabet or characters: each fits the language it writes.
tricks.body_zh: 字母也好、漢字也好：每一種都適合它所寫的語言。

activities.title_en: Keep the Class Accounts in Clay

materials.en: A lump of clay or play dough for each pair, about the size of a large cookie
materials.zh: 每兩人一塊黏土或紙黏土，大約一片大餅乾那麼大

materials.en: A chopstick or a craft stick with one end cut at a slant, to press wedges
materials.zh: 一支一端斜切的筷子或冰棒棍，用來壓出楔形

steps.en: Flatten the clay into a tablet that fits in your palm.
steps.zh: 把黏土壓成可以放在掌心的泥板。

steps.en: Count something real in the classroom: chairs, windows, people who walk to school. Write each count in Babylonian numbers: an upright wedge for each one, a corner wedge for each ten.
steps.zh: 數一數教室裡真的有的東西：椅子、窗戶、走路上學的人。用巴比倫的數字寫下每個數：一個直楔代表一，一個角楔代表十。

steps.en: Swap tablets with another pair. Read their numbers out in English: “There are twenty-six chairs.”
steps.zh: 和另一組交換泥板，用英文唸出他們的數字：「There are twenty-six chairs.」

steps.en: Now try to record what was counted, without using any letters or characters. How would you show “chairs”? How would you show your teacher's name?
steps.zh: 接著試著記下「數的是什麼」，但不可以用任何字母或漢字。「椅子」要怎麼表示？老師的名字又要怎麼表示？

activities.tip_en: Step 4 is the lesson. Students usually find that things are easy to draw and names are not, which is exactly the problem early writers solved by borrowing sounds.
activities.tip_zh: 第四步就是這堂課的重點。學生通常會發現：東西很好畫，名字卻畫不出來——這正是早期的書寫者借用聲音所解決的問題。

materials.en: Paper and colored pencils
materials.zh: 紙和色鉛筆

materials.en: The examples from the “A Picture, or a Sound?” game
materials.zh: 「是圖，還是聲音？」遊戲裡的例子

steps.en: Say your English name slowly and break it into sounds. “Ka-ren,” “Ben,” “Lu-key.”
steps.zh: 慢慢唸出你的英文名字，把它拆成幾個聲音。例如 Ka-ren、Ben、Lu-key。

steps.en: For each sound, find a word that sounds like it and is easy to draw: a car, a bee, a key.
steps.zh: 每一個聲音，找一個唸起來很像、又好畫的字：car（車）、bee（蜜蜂）、key（鑰匙）。

steps.en: Draw your name as a row of pictures. Trade with a classmate and read each other's names aloud.
steps.zh: 把名字畫成一排圖。和同學交換，把對方的名字唸出來。

steps.en: Try a Chinese name the same way. Is it easier or harder? Why?
steps.zh: 用同樣的方法試試中文名字。比較容易還是比較難？為什麼？

activities.tip_en: Some names will not work well. That is the point: picture-sounds are clumsy, which is one reason writing systems grew sets of signs used mainly for their sounds.
activities.tip_zh: 有些名字會畫得很勉強，這正是重點：用圖畫借聲音很笨拙，這也是文字系統後來發展出一套主要用來表音的記號的原因之一。

links.en: Why Did the First Cities Grow Beside Rivers?
links.zh: 最早的城市為什麼都在河邊？
links.note_en: Uruk, where the first tablets were written, was one of the first cities. Lesson 4 asks why cities grew where they did, beside four great rivers.
links.note_zh: 寫下第一批泥板的烏魯克，是最早的城市之一。第四課要問：城市為什麼出現在那四條大河旁邊？

links.zh: 人為什麼開始種田？
links.note_en: The granary that had to be counted.
links.note_zh: 那個需要清點的穀倉。

links.zh: 漢字從哪裡來？甲骨文到篆書
links.note_en: The oracle bones up close, and how the characters changed from bone to bronze to seal script.
